newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Some Russian refinery runs slip on oil exports.
newsitem.headline: Some Russian refinery runs slip on oil exports.

text.p: Russia's Fuel and Energy Ministry, which has boosted crude oil exports in the first quarter, is still worried about lower domestic refinery runs, industry sources said on Thursday.
Dmitry Kondakov, deputy head of the ministry's oil refining department, said some refineries, which were already working below capacity, had been undersupplied by 30 percent.
A ministry programme to ensure what he called adequate supplies had not been fully implemented, he said.
"I think you're going to see some reduction in runs, but not too great, within the next two to three weeks," said one senior Moscow-based oil trader.
Sources said runs were down at Volga and Urals area plants, the heart of Russia's refining sector.
"Runs are definitely down compared to recent months," a second trader said.
But sources said the phenomenon was probably temporary and that a long-term impact on net export volumes was unlikely.
The ministry may be worried, but it recently raised Russia's first quarter crude oil export volumes to 28.1 million tonnes from 25.7 million tonnes, an 18.6 percent increase year-on-year.

Government data obtained by Reuters showed refineries received 14.07 million tonnes (3.38 million barrels per day) of oil for processing in February, 240,000 tonnes (57,600 bpd), or 1.7 percent, below levels scheduled by the ministry and pipeline monopoly Transneft.

The Ufaneftekhim refinery, in the Urals, received 657,000 tonnes (157,700 bpd) last month, five percent less than scheduled. The refinery gets its oil from neighbouring independent oil producer Bashneft in Bashkiria.

The lower runs were enough to prompt the president of Bashkiria, an autonomous republic, to order on Wednesday that Bashneft stop oil exports to leave more for refineries, Interfax news agency said. Bashneft's 50,000 bpd exports in 1995 accounted for three percent of Russia's total.
The Novokyubyshev refinery in the lower Volga region got 685,075 tonnes (164,000 bpd) in February, or seven percent below government targets.
The Kyubyshev refinery got two percent more oil than scheduled, or 466,500 tonnes (112,000 bpd), but is working well below its 1996 refining average of 200,000 bpd.
"There is a rumour that YUKOS (Russia's second biggest oil company) is trying to prevent outsiders from refining at their facilities," one Russian source said. YUKOS owns the Kyubyshev refineries.
Deliveries of crude to the Volgograd refinery slipped 1.2 percent to 610,200 tonnes (146,500 bpd).
But the Saratov refinery in the lower Volga bucked the trend and boosted February crude oil supplies 22 percent over scheduled levels to 304,000 tonnes (73,000 bpd).
Russian oil shipments to Kazakh and Ukrainian refineries were nearly 13 percent below targeted levels, or 1.44 million tonnes (345,600 bpd).

Traders attributed the lower deliveries to pressured differentials for Russian heavy fuel oil in Europe, high domestic transport tariffs, logistics glitches as oil firms integrate upstream and downstream operations and the desire to export crude oil.
"People have been willing to pay a lot to get oil to export under the federal programmes," said the first trader, referring to a government export scheme offering tax breaks.
Russia's total refining capacity is 6.5 million barrels per day, but 28 major refineries typically only work at 50-60 percent of capacity.
Producers and traders boosted Russia's total crude oil exports in 1996 by nine percent to 2.1 million barrels per day.
"Mintop's (the ministry's) task is to ensure that a certain amount of crude oil output -- probably about 50 percent -- ends up in domestic refineries," said one trader at a Western firm.
-- Lynnley Browning, Moscow Newsroom, +7095 941 8520
